podcast.title: Creative Differences with Management
podcast.body: Brian Dorody, a holdover from Big Wreck, was initially excluded from the Thorneley lineup because management felt his presence would make the new band too similar to Big Wreck, aiming for Thorneley to be a "separate sort of thing." This decision added strain to relationships. "Brian was initially going to be the other guitar player in Thorneley. And then the sort of what's called the grown-ups, the people on the other side of the desk, where like, it's too much like Big Rec of Brian's around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Formation of the Band
podcast.body: After the first Big Wreck disbanded, Ian Thorneley moved to Toronto, got married, and began writing, leading to the formation of the band "Thorneley." The lineup, except for Brian Dorody, was new. "His relationship with Chad Kruger of Nickelback led him deciding with 604 Records out of Vancouver. And this was the beginning of a brand new band simply called Thorneley..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Touring and Lineup Changes
podcast.body: The band Thorneley engaged in tours, including one where guitarist Paula announced she would be absent for a gig in Edmonton due to her honeymoon. This unexpected vacancy led to Brian Dorody filling in, which subsequently contributed to the reformation of Big Wreck. "Paula was like, oh, by the way, that gig in Edmonton, I'm not going to be there. As I'm going on my honeymoon in Portugal..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Version Disbandment (2001-2002)
xref.body: The first iteration of Big Wreck concluded around 2001 or 2002, with Ian Thorneley subsequently pursuing other musical projects. "But that first version of the band was done by 2002."

xref.title: Ahmet Ertegun Anecdotes
xref.body: Ahmet Ertegun, co-founder of Atlantic Records, shared stories about Led Zeppelin with Ian Thorneley during a dinner meeting. "And then he gave me some Zeppelin stories."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Albatross Album Naming
xref.body: The album "Albatross" was named after its titular song, which itself was named when the word "Albatross" simply "fell into" Ian Thorneley's lap during writing, rather than a conscious reference to the Rime of the Ancient Mariner or John Cleese's sketch. The general practice for naming albums is to choose a song title, with "In Loving Memory" and "But for the Sun" being exceptions. "Dude, I just named the album after the song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Anecdotes with Ahmet Ertegun
xref.body: During Big Wreck's first iteration, Ian Thorneley had experiences with Ahmet Ertegun, co-founder of Atlantic Records, including a dinner at his office where Ertegun heard Big Wreck's music and shared stories about bands like the Rolling Stones and Led Zeppelin. Ertegun was described as a small Turkish man with a perfectly manicured mustache, often accompanied by "Amazonian gorgeous women." "Did you actually go for dinner with Ahmed Erdogan? Yeah, I mean, I was brought up to his office by Craig Calman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Band Members' Personality
xref.body: Ian Thorneley found the members of Velvet Revolver, including Slash, to be "really, really sweet and articulate and cool and down to earth," akin to any other band members he had toured with. "They were just like real dudes. They were real normal guys like any other band that I toured with before."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Chad Kroeger's Work Style
xref.body: Ian Thorneley respects Chad Kroeger's brilliance but notes that Kroeger's successful working style differs from his own. This difference sometimes led to external pressure from others trying to impose Kroeger's methods on Ian's projects. "But the way that he works is very different than the way that I work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Connection with Chad Kroeger
xref.body: Ian Thorneley has worked extensively with Chad Kroeger of Nickelback, considering him a close friend and family member. However, he acknowledges that Kroeger's successful working methods differ significantly from his own, leading to external pressures from those trying to replicate Kroeger's success. "But having said that, he, he, I, that I've worked a lot with the guy and he's like, he's like a family member and he's a very close guy and very close friend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Contrast between Industry 1.0 and 2.0
xref.body: Ian Thorneley noted a significant difference in the music industry between Big Wreck's first and second versions. The initial era involved experiences like being wined and dined by label executives such as Ahmet Ertegun, while the later period with SRO Anthem offered more creative freedom without the commercial pressures of chasing hits. "The music industry of Big Rec version 1.0. It was very different from what you had to deal with Big Rec version 2.0."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: David Gen Collaboration
xref.body: David Gen, who co-wrote the song "Make the Leave" for Ian Thorneley's "Tiny Pictures" album, also worked with Matt Good.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Early Business Exploitation Experience
xref.body: During the period with the band Thorneley, Ian encountered individuals in business who attempted to take advantage of him, leading to a significant phone conversation in 2005 or 2006 where his artistic and personal needs were dismissed. This experience taught him about the harsh realities of the music industry. "And the quote was, I don't give a fuck about your child."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Financial Worries and Motivation
xref.body: Despite his success, Ian Thorneley consistently experiences financial worries, especially with family responsibilities. This serves as a significant self-motivating mechanism, extending beyond purely artistic concerns to the practical needs of supporting his family. "I have, I have 11 month old at home, you know, and he's, he eats a lot of food. He eats more than I do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: First Velvet Revolver Consideration (Pre-Weiland)
xref.body: Before Scott Weiland joined Velvet Revolver, Ian Thorneley was considered as a potential singer. He received a CD with three instrumental tracks to write over, but he didn't pay much attention to it as his first Thorneley record was about to be released. "I remember getting a CD right before the first Thorneley record came out. I got a CD with three cuts on it, just instrumental tracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Ian Thorneley's Audition Experience
xref.body: Ian Thorneley rehearsed with Velvet Revolver in Los Angeles after Scott Weiland's departure. He found the musical aspect and chemistry to be strong, and the band members (Slash, Duff McKagan, etc.) to be "real dudes" and normal guys, contrary to any "reality show" perception. "It was really nice to see that. It wasn't, it wasn't the reality show, whatever that I had imagined it would be like."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Ian Thorneley's Session Work
xref.body: Ian Thorneley worked as a session player for Nickelback, among other artists, after the initial breakup of Big Wreck. "If you look in the line of notes for albums by Nickelback and Sarah Harmer and Stephen Fearing, you'll see his name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Jeff Burles' Role as Drummer
xref.body: Jeff Burles, drummer for The Tea Party, played drums for several Thorneley shows, including a significant gig in Edmonton, before the full reformation of Big Wreck. "Jeff Burles from the Tea Party was actually a drummer at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Live Wardrobe Malfunction
xref.body: During a Thorneley tour show in Edmonton or Calgary, possibly on Halloween, the power repeatedly went out due to running too many amps. While Ian was engaging the audience with jumps and antics, his pants split open in the crotch, revealing his anatomy due to not wearing underwear. His guitar tech, Shayne, attempted to tape him up, and a crew member named Timmy retrieved new pants, allowing him to finish the show. "And during one of these jumps, my pants split open in the crotchal area. And these days I didn't wear underwear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Post-Big Wreck Version 1.0 Career Transition
xref.body: After Big Wreck's initial disbandment around 2001-2002, Ian Thorneley moved back to Toronto and found work as a session player. He contributed to albums by artists such as Nickelback, Sarah Harmer, and Stephen Fearing. "After big rec version 1.0 broke up, Ian moved back to Toronto where he found work as a session player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Protecting Artistic Vision
xref.body: Ian Thorneley demonstrated a strong conviction in protecting his artistic output, which he likened to protecting his child. This conviction allowed him to resist manipulation and commercial pressures, distinguishing him from many musicians who might compromise for a living. "Now, what's, what I'm finding interesting is that this is your child, your baby. Yeah. And the conviction that you have in protecting your baby is not something that you see in a lot of musicians..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Reason for Rejecting Velvet Revolver Frontman Role
xref.body: Despite the musical chemistry and positive vibe during rehearsals, Ian Thorneley ultimately did not join Velvet Revolver. The band sought a "peacock" frontman in the vein of David Lee Roth or Scott Weiland, a role that didn't align with Ian's preference to play guitar on stage. "I'm not that comfortable doing the whole, you know, front guy tambourine thing. It's just not for me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Reformation as Big Wreck Version 2.0
xref.body: The band reunited around 2010-2011, initiated by Ian Thorneley missing the connection with former members. A Thorneley tour stop near Sarnia, where Brian Dorody lived, led to Dorody filling in for a show when the existing guitarist was unavailable, sparking the idea for a new Big Wreck era. "And then all of a sudden, there's Big Rec version 2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Search for a New Vocalist
xref.body: Velvet Revolver sought a new lead singer on two separate occasions: once before Scott Weiland joined, and again after his departure. Ian Thorneley was considered during both searches. "Looking for a guided replace Scott W Island. And somehow your name came up. So let's go through that story because I find this is fascinating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Shared "Guitarist First" Affliction with Ian Thorneley
xref.body: Miles Kennedy, known for singing with Slash and Alter Bridge, shares a long-standing history with Ian Thorneley and a common trait of primarily identifying as a guitarist rather than a singer, though Kennedy has since adapted to the frontman role without a guitar. "Oddly enough, like Miles, who sings with slash all the time, the, the mild and I go way back and, and we suffer from the same affliction where guitar players first and singers second."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Shared "Guitarist First" Affliction with Miles Kennedy
xref.body: Ian Thorneley notes a long-standing connection with Miles Kennedy, lead singer for Slash's solo band and Alter Bridge. They share the characteristic of being "guitar players first and singers second," although Kennedy has since embraced the frontman role without a guitar. "Oddly enough, like Miles, who sings with slash all the time, the, the mild and I go way back and, and we suffer from the same affliction where guitar players first and singers second."
